{{short description|When curves on a surface passing through a given point have the same normal curvature}}
[[File:Meusnier_theorem_color.png | thumb | right | Meusnier’s theorem, visualized]]
In [[differential geometry]], '''Meusnier's theorem''' states that all [[curve]]s on a [[surface (differential geometry)|surface]] passing through a given point ''p'' and having the same [[tangent line]] at ''p'' also have the same [[normal curvature]] at ''p'' and their [[osculating circle]]s form a sphere. The theorem was first announced by [[Jean Baptiste Meusnier]] in 1776, but not published until 1785.<ref>Jean Meusnier: ''Mém. prés. par div. Etrangers.'' Acad. Sci. Paris, 10  (1785)  pp.&nbsp;477–510</ref>
At least prior to 1912, several writers in English were in the habit of calling the result ''Meunier's theorem'', although there is no evidence that Meusnier himself ever spelt his name in this way.<ref>R. C. Archibald, [https://www.jstor.org/stable/3603070 Query 76], ''Mathematical Gazette'', 6 (May, 1912), p. 297</ref>
This alternative spelling of Meusnier's name also appears on the [[Names inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe|Arc de Triomphe]] in [[Paris]].
